newsitem.title: PERU: FEATURE - Peru slums a grim witness to economic hardship.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Peru slums a grim witness to economic hardship.

text.p: Maria Elena will cut your hair for a dollar. Her barber shop is a plastic chair on a dirt street, a battered mirror and some drawings of a variety of hair styles for men, all very short.
"I'm 18, no, 19," she said, narrowly avoiding giving away that she is working under age. She is about 13 and, like just under half of Peru's 23 million people, is dirt poor.

Stony dirt roads run by one-room shacks smelling vaguely of urine. This is the "Susana Higuchi Human Settlement," one of the sprawling shantytowns that surround Lima's better-off suburbs like a dirty egg white simmering around a richer yolk.

The settlement was named after President Alberto Fujimori's wife. Lima's "human settlements" are often named after famous people in the hope they will do something to help, but residents of Susana Higuchi may have backed the wrong horse. The president got a divorce and they still have no running water or sewers.

"Things are getting more difficult," said Nicolasa, who runs a small shop selling tinned tuna and Inca Cola, Peru's ubiquitous metallic-yellow soft drink. She and her husband earn just enough to feed themselves and their two children, and most people in Susana Higuchi scrape by on less than $100 a month.

"Things are hard, really hard," said Maria Elisabeth, who lives nearby, kneeling in the street washing clothes in a plastic bucket as her young children stood grinning around her. "I've just given birth so things are really tough now."
SPLUTTERS AFTER DISASTROUS 1980S

Despite coughs and splutters, Peru has grown strongly under Fujimori's free market policies, which ended the disastrous see-saws inflicted by populist governments in the 1980s. Growth has averaged five percent a year since 1991 and inflation has withered to 11.8 percent from 7,500 percent.

But economists say it will take many years of expansion to repair the legacy of decades of mismanagement and for the lot of millions of paupers to improve substantially. The government says 47 percent of Peruvians are poor and 19 percent extremely poor.

Some of Fujimori's policies actually made life tougher. Privatized companies fired workers and the government ended state subsidies that kept the prices of basic goods like bread and rice artificially low.

"The people who have suffered most from the austerity program, like in other parts of the world, have been those with the lowest incomes," Juan Jose Marthans, head of Lima University's economics department, said.
If the poor are to see any improvement soon, he said, Peru needs to grow faster than the five-or-so percent annual expansion widely foreseen for the next few years.
POPULISTS OUT OF STYLE

But few think the poor would benefit from a return to the populist policies of the recent past. Leading opposition congressman Carlos Chipoco argues more for tinkering with Fujimori's policies than for big changes.

"I think the situation of the poor in general has improved because there has been an end to hyperinflation and because there has been economic growth," he said. "But possibilities of improvement are still not available to the extremely poor."

Chipoco wants money from privatizations to be pumped into the financial system to spur further growth and tax incentives to lure investment to the countryside. The main export of many remote villages is currently people drifting to the cities.

"This is reality, this poverty," said Juan Encarnacion, a short man sliding into middle age as secretary of "The Little Trees Human Settlement" next door to Susana Higuchi. "If we were a bit better off, we would build our houses of bricks," he added.

Residents built the checkerboard of cube-shaped shacks themselves out of matting and chip board. There are no trees in The Little Trees settlement, just the usual dirt roads leading off a busy highway. There is electricity but no water or sewers.
Rising above the settlement, scuffed brown mountainsides covered with a rash of shantytowns stretch into the murky distance of Lima as far as the eye can see.
POOR OLD LIMA

Swollen by an arriving tide of peasants, Lima's population has increased more than tenfold over the past 50 years. The center still preserves the colonial grandeur of the viceroyalty of Peru, from which Spain ruled half of its Latin American possessions, but the great buildings are in disrepair and the streets are jammed with people selling food, sweets, tissues and whatever else they can.
Still, while the process is slow, the urban poor benefit more from economic growth than those in the country.

"If you want to tackle rural poverty seriously in Peru you have to build roads, you have to make sure the railways serve the places they should, you have to ensure water supplies. You have to make sure that the girl who would have to walk 12 miles (20 km) to get to school only has to walk one mile (1.6 km)," Oscar Jasaui, head of the Lima Chamber of Economists, said.
As the poor wait for growth to take effect, life is still tough at The Little Trees. There are not enough police to patrol its narrow streets so people take matters into their own hands.

"Sometimes we find thieves here in the night," Encarnacion said. "So we grab hold of them and we give them a people's trial. We don't kill them but we strip them and we just beat them up and the police come and take them away."
